question: Do creatures phasing back in trigger enter the battlefield abilities?
answer_gold: No. Phasing in is not a zone change, so it doesn't trigger "enters the battlefield" abilities (or any other zone-change triggers). The permanent was never treated as having left the battlefield in the first place, even though it was ignored while phased out.

question: how does trample work with deathtouch?
answer_gold: A trampling creature with deathtouch only needs to assign 1 damage to each blocking creature to count as "lethal damage" to it, then can assign all remaining damage to the defending player/planeswalker. Deathtouch redefines lethal damage: any nonzero amount of combat damage from a deathtouch source counts as lethal for the purpose of trample's damage-assignment rules, so the trampling creature doesn't need to assign damage equal to the blocker's toughness — 1 point per blocker satisfies the requirement.

question: is storm a triggered ability that can be countered?
answer_gold: Yes. Storm is a triggered ability that goes on the stack when you cast the spell with storm, and like any triggered ability it can be countered by an effect that specifically counters abilities (e.g. Stifle). It can't be countered by something that only counters spells, because a triggered ability on the stack isn't a spell.

question: can i use cards with hybrid mana symbols in a commander deck that only has one of those colors?
answer_gold: No, not unless the commander's color identity includes every color in that hybrid symbol. A hybrid mana symbol makes the card all of the colors of that symbol for every purpose, including color identity — it doesn't matter that you could pay the cost with only one of those colors of mana. So a card with a {W/U} symbol is both white and blue for deckbuilding purposes and needs both colors in the commander's color identity to be legal in that deck.

question: can I respond to the untap step?
answer_gold: No. No player receives priority during the untap step, so nothing can be cast or activated in response to it, and no one gets a window to respond to anything happening during it. Any ability that triggers during the untap step waits and goes on the stack the next time a player would get priority, usually during the upkeep step.

question: are creatures still considered attacking creatures during the end of combat step?
answer_gold: Yes. Creatures (and battles/planeswalkers) remain attacking/blocking throughout the end of combat step; they are only removed from combat at the very end of that step, right before it closes and the postcombat main phase begins. So any "as long as this creature is attacking" effect or ability that cares about attacking status is still live for the whole end of combat step.

question: Do you cast lands?
answer_gold: No, playing a land is not casting. It's a special action: you simply put the land onto the battlefield during a main phase when you have priority and the stack is empty, without using the stack. Because it never goes on the stack, a land is never a spell, and opponents can't respond to it with instants or activated abilities.

question: can I sacrifice an evoked creature before that creature's evoke triggered ability resolves?
answer_gold: Yes, you can sacrifice it (or otherwise get rid of it) through some other means before the evoke trigger resolves. The evoke trigger doesn't target — it just instructs its controller to sacrifice "it," i.e. that specific permanent. If that permanent is already gone from the battlefield by the time the ability resolves, there's simply nothing left to sacrifice: rule 701.21a defines sacrificing as moving a permanent you control from the battlefield to the graveyard, which is impossible once it isn't a permanent on the battlefield anymore. So the ability still resolves (it isn't countered), but that part of its effect does nothing.

question: if a card loses all abilities, does that include keyword abilities?
answer_gold: Yes. Keyword abilities (like flying, trample, deathtouch) are abilities — the keyword is just shorthand printed on the card for a full chunk of rules text or a defined ability. An effect that strips "all abilities" removes keyword abilities along with any other activated, triggered, or static abilities the object has.

question: can i draw cards if i'm already at my maximum hand size?
answer_gold: Yes. There's no rule stopping you from drawing (or otherwise gaining) cards past your maximum hand size during the turn. The maximum hand size is only enforced at cleanup: as part of your cleanup step you discard down to your maximum hand size (normally seven) if you're over it.

question: what happens when a planeswalker has 0 or less loyalty counters?
answer_gold: It's put into its owner's graveyard. This is a state-based action, checked and applied automatically whenever a player would receive priority — no one needs to do anything to make it happen, and it doesn't use the stack. Note the loyalty-0 state-based action as literally worded only triggers at exactly 0; a planeswalker can't actually go below 0 loyalty, since loyalty is a number of counters and removing more counters than are present just removes all of them, leaving it at 0.

question: do non-creature artifacts die?
answer_gold: Yes. The rules define "dies" generically for any permanent, not just creatures. Rule 700.4 is the entire definition: “The term dies means ‘is put into a graveyard from the battlefield.’” That wording isn't restricted to creatures, so a non-creature artifact that goes from the battlefield to a graveyard (destroyed, sacrificed, or otherwise) technically “dies” under the rules, just like a creature would. Players often use “dies” conversationally as if it only applied to creatures, but per the actual rules text it applies to any permanent, artifacts included.

question: what happens if i should draw a card when my library is empty?
answer_gold: You lose the game, but not instantly — it's applied as a state-based action the next time any player would receive priority. Rule 704.5b: “If a player attempted to draw a card from a library with no cards in it since the last time state-based actions were checked, that player loses the game.” Rule 121.4 describes the same event from the draw-action side: “A player who attempts to draw a card from a library with no cards in it loses the game the next time a player would receive priority.” So the attempted draw itself doesn't end the game on the spot; the loss is applied at the next state-based-action check, which normally happens right before the next priority window.

question: what are the steps in combat and when do I have priority as the defending player?
answer_gold: Combat has five steps, always in this order: beginning of combat, declare attackers, declare blockers, combat damage, and end of combat (rule 506.1). Declare blockers and combat damage are skipped if no creatures are attacking, and there are two combat damage steps if a first- or double-strike creature is involved. As the defending (non-active) player, you never get priority first in a step — the active player receives priority first, at the beginning of each step, after turn-based actions and step-triggered abilities are handled (rule 117.3a). Priority only moves to you after the active player takes an action and it resolves, or passes with the stack empty: rule 117.3d says “If a player has priority and chooses not to take any actions, that player passes... Then the next player in turn order receives priority.” In a two-player game, that next player is the defending player. So you get priority in every combat step, but always second, after the active player has acted or passed.

question: can i respond to a mana ability?
answer_gold: No. Mana abilities never use the stack, so there is no window in which anyone (including their own controller) can respond to them. Rule 605.3b: “An activated mana ability doesn’t go on the stack, so it can’t be targeted, countered, or otherwise responded to. Rather, it resolves immediately after it is activated.” Rule 605.4a says the same for triggered mana abilities: “A triggered mana ability doesn’t go on the stack, so it can’t be targeted, countered, or otherwise responded to. Rather, it resolves immediately after the mana ability that triggered it, without waiting for priority.”

question: can I respond to a cost being paid?
answer_gold: No. Paying a cost is part of the casting/activation process itself, and no player receives priority in the middle of that process — so there's no window to respond to a cost being paid. Rule 601.2 lays out casting as an ordered sequence: “Casting a spell includes proposal of the spell (rules 601.2a–d) and determination and payment of costs (rules 601.2f–h)... To cast a spell, a player follows the steps listed below, in order.” Rule 601.2g allows activating mana abilities to help pay, but those themselves can't be responded to either (see 605.3b/605.4a). Rule 601.2h: “The player pays the total cost... Partial payments are not allowed.” Only once 601.2a–h are fully complete does rule 601.2i kick in: “Once the steps described in 601.2a–h are completed... the spell becomes cast... If the spell’s controller had priority before casting it, they get priority.” No other player gets priority until the spell or ability is fully cast/activated and sitting on the stack — you can only respond to it at that point, not to the cost payment that produced it.

question: can you explain layers?
answer_gold: Layers are the fixed order the rules use to apply continuous effects when figuring out an object's current characteristics. Rule 613.1: “The values of an object’s characteristics are determined by starting with the actual object... Then all applicable continuous effects are applied in a series of layers in the following order.” The seven layers, in order, are: Layer 1 – copiable-value effects (613.1a); Layer 2 – control-changing effects (613.1b); Layer 3 – text-changing effects (613.1c); Layer 4 – type-changing effects (613.1d); Layer 5 – color-changing effects (613.1e); Layer 6 – ability-adding/removing effects and keyword counters (613.1f); Layer 7 – power/toughness-changing effects (613.1g). Effects are generally applied within a layer in timestamp order, layers 1 and 7 are further split into sublayers (613.2, 613.4), and dependency between effects can override timestamp order (613.8) — but the seven-layer order itself never changes.

question: how does the legend rule work?
answer_gold: If one player controls two or more legendary permanents that share the exact same name, that player must pick one to keep, and all the rest go straight to their owners' graveyards. Rule 704.5j (a state-based action): “If two or more legendary permanents with the same name are controlled by the same player, that player chooses one of them, and the rest are put into their owners’ graveyards. This is called the ‘legend rule.’” It only triggers on same name plus same controller — two different players can each control a legendary permanent with the same name with no conflict, and two differently-named legendary permanents controlled by one player are also fine.

question: when does my creature die after its been marked with a lethal amount of damage?
answer_gold: Not the instant the damage is marked — it dies the next time state-based actions are checked, which is right before any player would next receive priority. Rule 302.7: “Damage dealt to a creature by a source with neither wither nor infect is marked on that creature... If the total damage marked on that creature is greater than or equal to its toughness, that creature has been dealt lethal damage and is destroyed as a state-based action.” Rule 704.5g is the specific state-based action performing that destruction: “If a creature has toughness greater than 0, it has damage marked on it, and the total damage marked on it is greater than or equal to its toughness, that creature has been dealt lethal damage and is destroyed. Regeneration can replace this event.” Because of this, there can be a brief window — for example, mid-resolution of a spell or ability — where a creature is carrying lethal damage but hasn't actually died yet.

question: can I cast my commander from exile?
answer_gold: Not directly, no — rule 903.8 only lets you cast a commander from the command zone: “A player may cast a commander they own from the command zone.” There's no rule letting you cast a commander straight out of exile the way some cards let you cast things from exile. However, rule 903.9a gives you a path back: “If a commander is in a graveyard or in exile and that object was put into that zone since the last time state-based actions were checked, its owner may put it into the command zone. This is a state-based action.” That's optional and it's a move to the command zone, not a cast — you'd then cast it from there like normal, paying the commander tax under 903.8. So functionally you can usually get it back and cast it, but it always routes through the command zone, never directly from exile.

question: what happens during the cleanup step?
answer_gold: Two things happen automatically, and then usually nothing else (with one conditional exception). First, if the active player's hand has more cards than their maximum hand size (normally seven), they discard down to that number (rule 514.1). Second, simultaneously, all damage marked on permanents is removed and all “until end of turn” / “this turn” effects end (rule 514.2). Normally no player receives priority during cleanup, so nobody can cast spells or activate abilities (rule 514.3) — unless a state-based action would need to be performed or a triggered ability is waiting to go on the stack (including things that trigger “at the beginning of the next cleanup step”), in which case those are handled, the active player gets priority, a normal priority round happens, and once the stack empties and everyone passes, another cleanup step begins (rule 514.3a).

question: when are state-based actions checked?
answer_gold: State-based actions are checked every time a player would receive priority (and also during the cleanup step). Rule 704.3 spells out the loop: right before a player would get priority, the game checks the state-based-action conditions and performs any that apply, all simultaneously as a single event. If any were performed, the check repeats. Once a check produces no state-based actions, any waiting triggered abilities are put on the stack, and then the check repeats again. This continues until a check performs no state-based actions and no triggered abilities are waiting — only then does the appropriate player actually get priority. The same process runs during the cleanup step, except that if the first check there does nothing and nothing is waiting to trigger, no one gets priority and the step just ends.

question: when can I concede a game?
answer_gold: A player can concede at any time, in any game, for any reason — there's no restriction on timing. Conceding means leaving the game immediately and losing it (104.3a). This holds even if the player is currently under another player's control (e.g. from an effect that lets one player control another): the controller can't force the concession, but the controlled player can still choose to concede whenever they want (723.6).

question: how do I know who the active player is?
answer_gold: The active player is simply whoever's turn it currently is. Rule 102.1 defines it directly: "The active player is the player whose turn it is. The other players are nonactive players." The glossary entry for "Active Player" says the same thing in one line. There's no separate calculation — look at whose turn is in progress.

question: when someone other than the active player casts a spell, who gets priority first?
answer_gold: That same nonactive player who cast the spell gets priority again, first. Rule 117.3c is written generically for any player: "If a player has priority when they cast a spell, activate an ability, or take a special action, that player receives priority afterward." It doesn't matter whether the caster is the active player or not — whoever had priority and used it to cast the spell gets priority back before anyone else does (after the usual state-based-action/trigger check in 117.5).

question: when the active player cast a spell, who gets priority first?
answer_gold: The active player gets priority again first, since they're the one who cast the spell. Rule 117.3c applies regardless of active/nonactive status: "If a player has priority when they cast a spell, activate an ability, or take a special action, that player receives priority afterward." This is the same underlying rule as the mirror-image question about a nonactive player casting a spell (q026) — the rule doesn't distinguish active vs. nonactive; it's just "whoever cast it gets priority back."

question: can I hold priority to cast more spells after I've cast one or more spells?
answer_gold: Yes. Rule 117.3c gives you priority back immediately after you cast a spell (or activate an ability, or take a special action): "If a player has priority when they cast a spell, activate an ability, or take a special action, that player receives priority afterward." Since you have priority again, you're free to cast another spell (or several) before passing, which is what players mean by "holding priority." You only actually pass, and let the next player or the stack move, when you choose to per 117.3d.

question: when are lore counters put on sagas?
answer_gold: Lore counters go on a Saga at two points: when it enters the battlefield, and then again at the start of its controller's precombat main phase each turn. The gold field for this row (714.3a, 714.3c) only tells half the story: 714.3a is the entering-the-battlefield replacement effect, but it only applies to Sagas WITHOUT read ahead ("This Saga enters with a lore counter on it"). Sagas WITH read ahead instead use 714.3b, which lets the player choose a number between 1 and the Saga's final chapter number and enters with that many lore counters — that's a real, separate way lore counters get put on a Saga, and it's missing from the gold list. Then 714.3c is the recurring turn-based action: as a player's precombat main phase begins, they put a lore counter on each Saga they control with one or more chapter abilities, and this doesn't use the stack.

question: what is a delayed triggered ability?
answer_gold: A delayed triggered ability is a triggered ability that an effect creates during the game (usually while a spell or ability resolves, or when a replacement effect is applied) that will fire later, at some future event, rather than immediately. Per rule 603.7: "An effect may create a delayed triggered ability that can do something at a later time. A delayed triggered ability will contain 'when,' 'whenever,' or 'at,' although that word won't usually begin the ability." The glossary entry says the same thing concisely: it's an ability created by effects generated when some spells/abilities resolve or replacement effects apply, that does something later rather than at that time.

question: can non-permanent spells have abilities?
answer_gold: Yes. Instants and sorceries (the non-permanent spell types) primarily carry "spell abilities": per 113.3a, any text on an instant or sorcery spell is a spell ability — instructions followed while the spell resolves — unless it's actually an activated ability, a triggered ability, or a static ability that fits the exceptions in rule 113.6. So a non-permanent spell CAN have activated, triggered, or static abilities too, in the specific cases 113.6 lists (e.g. an ability that restricts how the spell can be cast, or one that says the spell can't be countered, functions on the stack per 113.6e/113.6g). Normally though, abilities of non-permanent objects like instants/sorceries only function while on the stack, unlike permanents whose abilities function on the battlefield (113.6's general framing).

question: can I use a mana ability when a spell with split-second is on the stack?
answer_gold: Yes. Split second (702.61a) blocks players from casting other spells or activating abilities that AREN'T mana abilities while the split-second spell is on the stack: "'Split second' means 'As long as this spell is on the stack, players can't cast other spells or activate abilities that aren't mana abilities.'" Rule 702.61b makes the mana-ability carve-out explicit: "Players may activate mana abilities and take special actions while a spell with split second is on the stack. Triggered abilities trigger and are put on the stack as normal while a spell with split second is on the stack." So mana abilities (and special actions) are untouched by split second; only non-mana activated abilities and casting other spells are locked out.

question: How many zones does the game normally use, and which of them belong to one player rather than being shared by everyone?
answer_gold: Normally seven: library, hand, battlefield, graveyard, stack, exile, and command (some older cards also use an eighth, the ante zone). Each player has their own library, hand, and graveyard. The battlefield, stack, exile, and command zone are shared areas that all players use together.

cr_quotes.400.1: A zone is a place where objects can be during a game. There are normally seven zones: library, hand, battlefield, graveyard, stack, exile, and command. Some older cards also use the ante zone. Each player has their own library, hand, and graveyard. The other zones are shared by all players.

question: Is a player's library a hidden zone or a public one, and can a player look through or rearrange the order of their own library whenever they like?
answer_gold: The library is a hidden zone -- even if every card in it happened to be revealed, it would still legally count as hidden information. And no, a player can't casually look at or rearrange the order of cards in their own library; it has to be kept as a single face-down pile whose order only changes when a specific rule or effect allows it.

cr_quotes.400.2: Public zones are zones in which all players can see the cards' faces... Hidden zones are zones in which not all players can be expected to see the cards' faces. Library and hand are hidden zones, even if all the cards in one such zone happen to be revealed.
cr_quotes.401.2: Each library must be kept in a single face-down pile. Players can't look at or change the order of cards in a library.

question: Are cards a player has exiled public information by default, or can a player keep them secret?
answer_gold: Public by default. Exile is listed among the public zones, and exiled cards are kept face up and may be examined by any player at any time, unless the specific spell or ability that exiled a card said it goes to exile face down.

cr_quotes.400.2: Graveyard, battlefield, stack, exile, ante, and command are public zones.
cr_quotes.406.3: Exiled cards are, by default, kept face up and may be examined by any player at any time. Cards "exiled face down" can't be examined by any player except when instructions allow it.

question: When a permanent is destroyed and moves from the battlefield to the graveyard, is it still the same game object it was on the battlefield, or does something change about its identity?
answer_gold: It becomes a new object with no memory of, or relation to, its previous existence, except for a short list of specific exceptions (like abilities that specifically look for the new object in the zone it moved to, or last-known-information rules). So an ability that cared about "that permanent" while it was on the battlefield generally can't follow it into the graveyard as the same thing.

cr_quotes.400.7: An object that moves from one zone to another becomes a new object with no memory of, or relation to, its previous existence. This rule has the following exceptions.

question: If an effect would put an instant or sorcery card onto the battlefield, what actually happens to it?
answer_gold: Nothing changes zones -- the card simply remains in whatever zone it was already in. Instants and sorceries are card types that can never exist on the battlefield, so an attempt to put one there just fails and it stays put.

cr_quotes.400.4a: If an instant or sorcery card would enter the battlefield, it remains in its previous zone.

question: If a token is moved off the battlefield (to a hand, graveyard, exile, or anywhere else), what happens to it, and can it ever come back?
answer_gold: A token that's in any zone other than the battlefield ceases to exist, as a state-based action -- though any triggered abilities that care about it changing zones do get a chance to trigger first, since that check happens before the token actually disappears. Once it has left the battlefield, a token can't come back or move to yet another zone; if something would try to move it again, it just stays where it is until the next state-based action check makes it cease to exist.

cr_quotes.111.7: A token that's in a zone other than the battlefield ceases to exist. This is a state-based action; see rule 704. (Note that if a token changes zones, applicable triggered abilities will trigger before the token ceases to exist.)
cr_quotes.111.8: A token that has left the battlefield can't move to another zone or come back onto the battlefield. If such a token would change zones, it remains in its current zone instead. It ceases to exist the next time state-based actions are checked; see rule 704.

question: Can players freely rearrange the order of objects on the stack, the way they might rearrange permanents on the battlefield?
answer_gold: No. The order of objects on the stack (like the order of a library or graveyard) can't be changed except when a specific effect or rule allows it. This is different from other zones like the battlefield, where a player can arrange their own permanents however they find convenient.

cr_quotes.400.5: The order of objects in a library, in a graveyard, or on the stack can't be changed except when effects or rules allow it. The same is true for objects arranged in face-down piles in other zones. Other objects in other zones can be arranged however their owners wish...

question: Does every turn always include all five phases (beginning, precombat main, combat, postcombat main, ending), even if nothing happens during some of them?
answer_gold: Yes. A turn consists of exactly those five phases in that order, and each one takes place every turn even if nothing happens during it -- for example, an uneventful combat phase with no attackers still occurs, it just passes quickly since its steps that require attacking creatures are skipped.

cr_quotes.500.1: A turn consists of five phases, in this order: beginning, precombat main, combat, postcombat main, and ending. Each of these phases takes place every turn, even if nothing happens during the phase. The beginning, combat, and ending phases are further broken down into steps, which proceed in order.

question: In a two-player game, does the player who takes the very first turn get a draw step on that turn?
answer_gold: No. In a two-player game, the player who plays first skips the draw step of their first turn -- they don't draw a card on turn one.

cr_quotes.103.8a: In a two-player game, the player who plays first skips the draw step (see rule 504, "Draw Step") of their first turn.

question: In a free-for-all multiplayer game with three or more players (not Two-Headed Giant), does the starting player skip the draw step of their first turn the way a starting player would in a two-player game?
answer_gold: No. That skip is specific to two-player games (and, in modified form, to Two-Headed Giant). In any other multiplayer game, no player skips the draw step of their first turn -- the starting player draws normally on turn one.

cr_quotes.103.8c: In all other multiplayer games, no player skips the draw step of their first turn.
cr_quotes.800.7: 800.7. In a multiplayer game other than a Two-Headed Giant game, the starting player doesn’t skip the draw step of their first turn. In a Two-Headed Giant game, the team who plays first skips the draw step of their first turn. See rule 103.8.

question: In a Two-Headed Giant game, does the team that takes the first turn skip its draw step, and if a step isn't skipped, does each player on a team normally draw their own card during that team's draw step?
answer_gold: Yes to both parts, but they're separate rules. The team that plays first skips the draw step of its first turn entirely, so neither player on that team draws for turn one. On any other turn, when the draw step isn't skipped, each player on the active team draws their own card during that shared draw step -- it isn't just one draw for the whole team.

cr_quotes.103.8b: In a Two-Headed Giant game, the team who plays first skips the draw step of their first turn.
cr_quotes.805.4b: Each player on a team draws a card during that team's draw step.
cr_quotes.810.6: 810.6. The team who plays first skips the draw step of its first turn.

question: If a player is given several extra turns at once by different effects, in what order are those extra turns actually taken?
answer_gold: Extra turns are added one at a time, directly after the specified turn, and the most recently created extra turn is the one taken first. So if two effects each grant an extra turn, the second effect's extra turn happens before the first effect's extra turn, because it was slotted in closer to the current turn.

cr_quotes.500.7: Some effects can give a player extra turns. They do this by adding the turns directly after the specified turn. If a player is given multiple extra turns, the extra turns are added one at a time. If multiple players are given extra turns, the extra turns are added one at a time, in APNAP order (see rule 101.4). The most recently created turn will be taken first.

question: If an effect would cause a player to skip their next upkeep, but their upkeep has already started by the time that effect resolves, does the upkeep get retroactively skipped?
answer_gold: No. Once a step, phase, or turn has actually started, it's too late to skip it -- a skip effect that arrives after the fact just waits and applies to the next occurrence of that step, phase, or turn instead.

cr_quotes.614.10: An effect that causes a player to skip an event, step, phase, or turn is a replacement effect. "Skip [something]" is the same as "Instead of doing [something], do nothing." Once a step, phase, or turn has started, it can no longer be skipped -- any skip effects will wait until the next occurrence.

question: If several triggered abilities controlled by different players all trigger from the same event, in what order are they put on the stack?
answer_gold: The active player's triggered abilities go on the stack first (so they end up on the bottom, resolving last among the group), and then each nonactive player's triggered abilities go on in turn order after that (ending up on top, resolving first). If a single player controls more than one of the simultaneously triggered abilities, that player chooses the order among their own.

cr_quotes.603.3b: If multiple abilities have triggered since the last time a player received priority, the abilities are placed on the stack in a two-part process. First, each player, in APNAP order, puts each triggered ability they control with a trigger condition that isn't another ability triggering on the stack in any order they choose... If a player controls more than one of these objects, that player chooses their relative order on the stack.

question: Because the active player's simultaneously-triggered abilities are placed on the stack before a nonactive player's, does that mean the active player's version of the trigger actually resolves first or last relative to the nonactive player's?
answer_gold: Last. The stack resolves top-down, and the active player's triggers are placed on the stack first (going to the bottom of that batch), with each nonactive player's triggers placed afterward (going on top). Since the stack keeps track of order and the top (most recently added) object resolves first when everyone passes, the nonactive player's trigger from that shared event actually resolves before the active player's does.

cr_quotes.603.3b: First, each player, in APNAP order, puts each triggered ability they control with a trigger condition that isn't another ability triggering on the stack in any order they choose.
cr_quotes.405.2: The stack keeps track of the order that spells and/or abilities were added to it. Each time an object is put on the stack, it's put on top of all objects already there.
cr_quotes.405.5: When all players pass in succession, the top (last-added) spell or ability on the stack resolves.

question: Do static abilities ever get put on the stack the way triggered and activated abilities do?
answer_gold: No. Static abilities continuously generate their effects and never go on the stack -- there's no window where a static ability is "resolving" or can be responded to the way a spell or a triggered/activated ability can.

cr_quotes.405.6b: Static abilities continuously generate effects and don't go on the stack. (See rule 604, "Handling Static Abilities.") This includes characteristic-defining abilities such as "[This object] is red" (see rule 604.3).

question: If a targeted spell or ability is about to resolve and every single one of its targets has become illegal, what happens to it?
answer_gold: It doesn't resolve at all. It's removed from the stack, and if it's a spell, put into its owner's graveyard, without doing anything. This is checked as the very first step of resolution, before any of its instructions are carried out.

cr_quotes.608.2b: If the spell or ability specifies targets, it checks whether the targets are still legal... If all its targets, for every instance of the word "target," are now illegal, the spell or ability doesn't resolve. It's removed from the stack and, if it's a spell, put into its owner's graveyard.

question: If a spell has two targets and only one of them becomes illegal before it resolves, does the whole spell fail, or does it still resolve and just skip the illegal target?
answer_gold: It still resolves, as long as at least one target remains legal. The spell affects its legal targets normally; the parts of its effect meant for the illegal target simply don't happen to that target, but everything else the spell does still occurs.

cr_quotes.608.2b: Otherwise, the spell or ability will resolve normally. Illegal targets, if any, won't be affected by parts of a resolving spell's effect for which they're illegal. Other parts of the effect for which those targets are not illegal may still affect them.

question: If an effect lets a player "choose new targets" for a spell or ability, must every one of the original targets actually be replaced?
answer_gold: No. The player may leave any number of the original targets unchanged, even if a target left unchanged would be illegal. If they do choose to change some or all of the targets, though, the new ones must be legal and can't cause any of the unchanged targets to become illegal.

cr_quotes.115.7d: If an effect allows a player to "choose new targets" for a spell or ability, the player may leave any number of the targets unchanged, even if those targets would be illegal. If the player chooses to change some or all of the targets, the new targets must be legal and must not cause any unchanged targets to become illegal.

question: If an effect lets a player "change the target(s)" of a spell (as opposed to "choose new targets"), can they change a target to something that isn't a legal target for that spell?
answer_gold: No, a target can only be changed to another legal target. If a given target can't be changed to another legal target, that original target is left unchanged (even if it's illegal by then), and if not all the targets can be changed to other legal targets, none of them are changed at all.

cr_quotes.115.7a: If an effect allows a player to "change the target(s)" of a spell or ability, each target can be changed only to another legal target. If a target can't be changed to another legal target, the original target is unchanged, even if the original target is itself illegal by then. If all the targets aren't changed to other legal targets, none of them are changed.

question: Can a spell or ability on the stack ever legally target itself?
answer_gold: No. A spell or ability on the stack is defined as an illegal target for itself, so nothing can be written or worded in a way that makes it a legal self-target.

cr_quotes.115.5: A spell or ability on the stack is an illegal target for itself.

question: If a spell or ability requires targets but its wording lets the caster choose any number of them, is choosing zero targets a legal choice, and if zero are chosen, is that spell or ability still considered "targeted"?
answer_gold: Choosing zero can be legal for that kind of wording, and in that case the spell or ability is not actually targeted -- it's only considered targeted if one or more targets were actually chosen for it, even though the rules still describe it as a spell or ability that "requires" targets.

cr_quotes.115.6: A spell or ability that requires targets may allow zero targets to be chosen. Such a spell or ability is still said to require targets, but that spell or ability is targeted only if one or more targets have been chosen for it.

question: What single word most commonly marks an effect as a replacement effect rather than some other kind of continuous effect?
answer_gold: The word "instead." Most replacement effects use "instead" to indicate that one event is being swapped out for a different modified event; a smaller set use the word "skip" for the same purpose (skipping something being treated as replacing it with nothing).

cr_quotes.614.1a: Effects that use the word "instead" are replacement effects. Most replacement effects use the word "instead" to indicate what events will be replaced with other events.

question: Can a replacement effect be created (by casting a spell or activating an ability) after the event it's meant to replace has already happened, and still change that outcome?
answer_gold: No. Replacement effects must exist before the event they'd modify actually occurs -- they can't reach back in time and change something that's already happened. That's why a player has to regenerate a creature in response to the spell that would destroy it, rather than after that spell has already resolved and destroyed it.

cr_quotes.614.4: Replacement effects must exist before the appropriate event occurs -- they can't "go back in time" and change something that's already happened. Spells or abilities that generate these effects are often cast or activated in response to whatever would produce the event and thus resolve before that event would occur.

question: If a permanent has an effect like "if a creature you control would deal damage to a player, it deals double that damage instead," does that replacement effect apply once, or does it keep reapplying to its own already-doubled result?
answer_gold: Just once. A replacement effect doesn't invoke itself repeatedly on the modified event it just created -- it only gets one opportunity to affect a given event (or a modified version of that event created by some other effect). So a single doubling effect turns 2 damage into 4, not an infinite cascade.

cr_quotes.614.5: A replacement effect doesn't invoke itself repeatedly; it gets only one opportunity to affect an event or any modified events that may replace that event.

question: If a source would deal 0 damage, and an effect says damage from that source would instead be increased or redirected, does that replacement effect do anything?
answer_gold: No. If a source deals 0 damage, it isn't considered to deal damage at all, so there's no damage-dealing event for a replacement effect to latch onto. Replacement effects that would increase that damage or send it somewhere else simply have nothing to replace, so they do nothing.

cr_quotes.614.7a: If a source would deal 0 damage, it does not deal damage at all. Replacement effects that would increase the damage dealt by that source, or would have that source deal that damage to a different object or player, have no event to replace, so they have no effect.

question: Is regeneration a triggered ability that goes on the stack, or is it a replacement effect?
answer_gold: It's a replacement effect, even though the printed reminder text doesn't literally contain the word "instead." "Regenerate [permanent]" is rules-shorthand for "the next time [permanent] would be destroyed this turn, instead remove all damage marked on it and tap it (and remove it from combat if applicable)" -- the word "instead" is implicit in the definition, and the shield doesn't use the stack the way a triggered ability would.

cr_quotes.614.8: Regeneration is a destruction-replacement effect. The word "instead" doesn't appear on the card but is implicit in the definition of regeneration. "Regenerate [permanent]" means "The next time [permanent] would be destroyed this turn, instead remove all damage marked on it and its controller taps it. If it's an attacking or blocking creature, remove it from combat."

question: Is an effect that tells a player to "skip" a step, phase, or turn a replacement effect, or some other kind of effect?
answer_gold: It's a replacement effect. Effects that use the word "skip" indicate that a step, phase, or turn is being replaced with nothing -- "skip [something]" is functionally the same as "instead of doing [something], do nothing."

cr_quotes.614.1b: Effects that use the word "skip" are replacement effects. These replacement effects use the word "skip" to indicate what events, steps, phases, or turns will be replaced with nothing.
cr_quotes.614.10: An effect that causes a player to skip an event, step, phase, or turn is a replacement effect. "Skip [something]" is the same as "Instead of doing [something], do nothing."

question: Are self-replacement effects (where part of a resolving spell's own effect replaces the rest of that same effect) continuous effects that exist independently on the battlefield, the same way most replacement effects do?
answer_gold: No. Self-replacement effects aren't continuous effects at all -- they're just part of a resolving spell or ability's own effect, replacing part or all of that same spell or ability's effect as it resolves. When applying replacement effects to an event, self-replacement effects are applied before any other (continuous) replacement effects.

cr_quotes.614.15: Some replacement effects are not continuous effects. Rather, they are an effect of a resolving spell or ability that replace part or all of that spell or ability's own effect(s). Such effects are called self-replacement effects... When applying replacement effects to an event, self-replacement effects are applied before other replacement effects.

question: When one permanent becomes a copy of another, does it also copy the counters, marked damage, and other continuous effects that happened to be affecting the original at that moment?
answer_gold: No. Copying only transfers the copiable values derived from the object's printed (or token-defined) text -- name, mana cost, color indicator, types, rules text, power/toughness, loyalty, and so on, as modified by other copy effects and by certain "as this enters" abilities. Status, counters and stickers are explicitly excluded from what gets copied. Marked damage isn't copied either, but for a different reason -- damage is merely marked on a permanent, so it was never one of the copiable values in the first place.

cr_quotes.707.2: The copiable values are the values derived from the text printed on the object (that text being name, mana cost, color indicator, card type, subtype, supertype, rules text, power, toughness, and/or loyalty), as modified by other copy effects, by its face-down status, and by "as . . . enters" and "as . . . is turned face up" abilities that set power and toughness (and may also set additional characteristics). Other effects (including type-changing and text-changing effects), status, counters, and stickers are not copied.
cr_quotes.120.3e: 120.3e Damage dealt to a creature by a source with neither wither nor infect causes that much damage to be marked on that creature.

question: If a token enters the battlefield as a copy of a permanent that has an enters-the-battlefield triggered ability, does that trigger actually fire for the token?
answer_gold: Yes. An object that enters the battlefield "as a copy" of another object becomes the copy as it enters -- it doesn't enter first and then become a copy afterward. So any enters-the-battlefield triggered abilities in the copied text get a normal chance to trigger, and any replacement effects that modify how the permanent enters (like "enters with" abilities) apply too.

cr_quotes.707.5: An object that enters the battlefield "as a copy" or "that's a copy" of another object becomes a copy as it enters the battlefield. It doesn't enter the battlefield, and then become a copy of that permanent. If the text that's being copied includes any abilities that replace the enters-the-battlefield event (such as "enters with" or "as [this] enters" abilities), those abilities will take effect. Also, any enters-the-battlefield triggered abilities of the copy will have a chance to trigger.

question: If permanent B has already become a copy of permanent A, and permanent A's copiable characteristics change afterward, does permanent B automatically update to match?
answer_gold: No. Once an object has been copied, changing the copiable values of the original object afterward doesn't cause the existing copy to change. The copy locked in the copiable values at the moment it copied the original; it doesn't keep tracking the original going forward.

cr_quotes.707.2b: Once an object has been copied, changing the copiable values of the original object won't cause the copy to change.

question: If an effect creates a copy of a spell that's on the stack, is that copy considered to have been "cast," the way the original spell was?
answer_gold: No. To copy a spell means to put a copy of it onto the stack directly; a copy of a spell isn't cast (and a copy of an activated ability isn't activated). That copy is a spell in its own right once it's on the stack, but the act of copying it is not the same event as casting it, which matters for anything that specifically cares about spells being cast.

cr_quotes.707.10: To copy a spell, activated ability, or triggered ability means to put a copy of it onto the stack; a copy of a spell isn't cast and a copy of an activated ability isn't activated.

question: If a permanent spell (one that's still on the stack) is itself a copy of another permanent spell, what does it turn into as it resolves and moves to the battlefield?
answer_gold: It becomes a token permanent as it's put onto the battlefield -- it's no longer treated as "a copy of a spell" once it resolves, and it isn't considered "created" for the purposes of rules or effects that care about tokens being created.

cr_quotes.608.3f: If the object that's resolving is a copy of a permanent spell, it will become a token permanent as it is put onto the battlefield in any of the steps above. A token put onto the battlefield this way is no longer a copy of a spell and is not "created" for the purposes of any rules or effects that refer to creating a token.
cr_quotes.707.10f: Some effects copy a permanent spell. As that copy resolves, it ceases being a copy of a spell and becomes a token permanent. (See rule 608.3f.)

question: If an object has a pair of linked abilities (where one ability refers only to things the other one did), and that object is copied, do the two abilities stay linked to each other on the copy?
answer_gold: Yes. If a pair of linked abilities is copied, they remain linked to one another on the object that copied them -- the linked ability still only refers to actions taken or objects affected by its own linked partner on that same copy, and it can't become linked to some other, unrelated ability the copy might also have.

cr_quotes.707.7: If a pair of linked abilities are copied, those abilities will be similarly linked to one another on the object that copied them. One ability refers only to actions that were taken or objects that were affected by the other. They can't be linked to any other ability, regardless of what other abilities the copy may currently have or may have had in the past.

question: What makes a game a "multiplayer game" under the rules -- is it about how many players began the game, or how many are still in it right now?
answer_gold: It's about how the game began. A multiplayer game is defined as a game that begins with more than two players, which fixes its status at the start. Nothing in that definition depends on how many players are still around later.

cr_quotes.800.1: A multiplayer game is a game that begins with more than two players. This section contains additional optional rules that can be used for multiplayer play.

question: In a multiplayer game played between teams, who counts as a given player's opponents?
answer_gold: All players who are not on that player's team. Teammates are the other players sharing the same team; everyone else in the game is an opponent, regardless of how many teams there are.

cr_quotes.102.3: In a multiplayer game between teams, a player's teammates are the other players on their team, and the player's opponents are all players not on their team.

question: If a spell or ability uses the phrase "your team," and the game in question isn't a multiplayer team game, who does "your team" actually refer to?
answer_gold: Just you. "Your team" is shorthand for "you and/or your teammates," but in a game that isn't a multiplayer game played between teams, there are no teammates to speak of, so "your team" means exactly the same thing as "you."

cr_quotes.102.4: A spell or ability may use the term "your team" as shorthand for "you and/or your teammates." In a game that isn't a multiplayer game between teams, "your team" means the same thing as "you."

question: What is each team's starting life total in a Two-Headed Giant game?
answer_gold: 30, shared between the two teammates as a single team life total, rather than the normal 20 each player would start with in a regular game.

cr_quotes.103.4a: In a Two-Headed Giant game, each team's starting life total is 30.

question: What is each player's starting life total in a Commander game?
answer_gold: 40, rather than the normal 20 used in a standard game.

cr_quotes.103.4c: In a Commander game, each player's starting life total is 40.

question: When a player leaves a multiplayer game (for example, by losing), what happens to the objects that player owns?
answer_gold: All objects that player owns leave the game along with them, and any effects giving that player control of other objects or players end. If any objects on the stack that aren't represented by cards were controlled by that player, those cease to exist; anything else that player still controlled at that point is exiled instead. None of this is a state-based action -- it happens immediately as soon as the player leaves.

cr_quotes.800.4a: When a player leaves the game, all objects (see rule 109) owned by that player leave the game and any effects which give that player control of any objects or players end. Then, if that player controlled any objects on the stack not represented by cards, those objects cease to exist. Then, if there are any objects still controlled by that player, those objects are exiled. This is not a state-based action. It happens as soon as the player leaves the game.

question: If an effect would change control of an object to a player who has already left a multiplayer game, does that control change actually happen?
answer_gold: No. If an object would change to the control of a player who has left the game, it simply doesn't. The same goes for tokens that would be created, or objects that would enter the battlefield or the stack, under that departed player's control -- none of those things happen for a player who's no longer in the game.

cr_quotes.800.4b: If an object would change to the control of a player who has left the game, it doesn't. If a token would be created under the control of a player who has left the game, no token is created. If an object would be put onto the battlefield or onto the stack under the control of a player who has left the game, that object remains in its current zone. If a player would be controlled by a player who has left the game, they aren't.

question: If a triggered ability would be controlled by a player who has already left a multiplayer game, does it get put on the stack?
answer_gold: No. If a triggered ability that would be controlled by a player who has left the game would be put onto the stack, it simply isn't put there at all.

cr_quotes.800.4d: If an object that would be owned by a player who has left the game would be created in any zone, it isn't created. If a triggered ability that would be controlled by a player who has left the game would be put onto the stack, it isn't put on the stack.

question: In a multiplayer game, does the very first mulligan a player takes count toward how many cards they'll have to put on the bottom of their library, the way it would in a two-player game?
answer_gold: No. In a multiplayer game (and in any Brawl game), the first mulligan a player takes is free -- it doesn't count toward the number of cards that player will bottom or the number of mulligans they're considered to have taken. Only their second and later mulligans count normally toward those totals.

cr_quotes.103.5c: In a multiplayer game and in any Brawl game, the first mulligan a player takes doesn't count toward the number of cards that player will put on the bottom of their library or the number of mulligans that player may take. Subsequent mulligans are counted toward these numbers as normal.

question: Does the multiplayer "free first mulligan" rule apply in a two-player Commander game?
answer_gold: No. The free-first-mulligan exception is written for "a multiplayer game," and a multiplayer game is specifically defined as one that begins with more than two players. A two-player Commander game (even with its 40 life and singleton deck) doesn't meet that definition, so every mulligan a player takes there counts toward the cards they must put on the bottom of their library, starting with the first one.

cr_quotes.103.5c: In a multiplayer game and in any Brawl game, the first mulligan a player takes doesn't count toward the number of cards that player will put on the bottom of their library or the number of mulligans that player may take.
cr_quotes.800.1: A multiplayer game is a game that begins with more than two players.

question: Under the limited range of influence option, can a player's creature attack an opponent who is outside that player's range of influence?
answer_gold: No. Creatures can only attack opponents within their controller's range of influence, planeswalkers controlled by those opponents, and battles those opponents protect. If a player has no opponents within range, their creatures simply can't attack at all that combat.

cr_quotes.801.3: Creatures can attack only opponents within their controller's range of influence, planeswalkers controlled by those opponents, and battles protected by those opponents. If no opponents are within a player's range of influence, creatures that player controls can't attack.

question: In a Two-Headed Giant game (which uses the shared team turns option), does each player on the active team draw their own card during the team's shared draw step, or is there just one draw for the whole team?
answer_gold: Each player on the team draws their own card. The team shares a single draw step, but the drawing itself is still done individually by each player on that team -- it's not a single shared draw for the pair.

cr_quotes.805.4b: Each player on a team draws a card during that team's draw step.

question: If a player leaves a multiplayer game while controlling a permanent that has a leaves-the-battlefield triggered ability, does that ability trigger, and does it go on the stack?
answer_gold: It triggers, but it isn't put on the stack. The player's departure moves their permanents out of the game, so the trigger condition is met -- but a triggered ability that would be controlled by a player who has left the game is never put onto the stack, so its effect simply never happens. The rules use exactly that split: the ability triggers, and it isn't put on the stack.

cr_quotes.800.4a: When a player leaves the game, all objects (see rule 109) owned by that player leave the game...
cr_quotes.603.6c: Some leaves-the-battlefield abilities are written as intervening-if triggered abilities to reflect that they don't trigger if the permanent leaves the battlefield and returns to the battlefield as a result of the same event, such as with an effect that exiles a permanent and returns it to the battlefield in the same resolution.
cr_quotes.800.4d:
800.4d If an object that would be owned by a player who has left the game would be created in any zone, it isn’t created. If a triggered ability that would be controlled by a player who has left the game would be put onto the stack, it isn’t put on the stack.
Example: Astral Slide is an enchantment that reads, “Whenever a player cycles a card, you may exile target creature. If you do, return that creature to the battlefield under its owner’s control at the beginning of the next end step.” During Alex’s turn, Bianca uses Astral Slide’s ability to exile Alex’s Hypnotic Specter. Before the end of that turn, Bianca leaves the game. At the beginning of the end step, the delayed triggered ability generated by Astral Slide that would return Hypnotic Specter to the battlefield triggers, but it isn’t put on the stack. Hypnotic Specter never returns to the battlefield.

question: If a game-restarting effect ends a multiplayer game and starts a new one, and one of the original players had already left the game (lost) before the restart happened, is that departed player included in the new game?
answer_gold: No. The rule for restarting the game specifies that all players in the game when it ended start the new game -- a player who already left before the game ended is not among "the players in that game when it ended," so they don't come back for the restarted game.

cr_quotes.727.1: A game that is restarted immediately ends. No players in that game win, lose, or draw that game. All players in that game when it ended then start a new game following the procedures set forth in rule 103, "Starting the Game"...

question: Does activating a mana ability use up a player's priority the way casting a spell would, or can the same player still act again immediately afterward?
answer_gold: It doesn't cost them anything -- activating a mana ability is one of the actions covered by the general priority rule that gives a player priority right back after they cast a spell, activate an ability, or take a special action. Since a mana ability also never uses the stack and resolves immediately, its activator ends up right back with priority afterward, free to pass or do something else, rather than the turn simply moving on to the next player.

cr_quotes.117.3c: If a player has priority when they cast a spell, activate an ability, or take a special action, that player receives priority afterward.
cr_quotes.605.3b: An activated mana ability doesn't go on the stack, so it can't be targeted, countered, or otherwise responded to. Rather, it resolves immediately after it is activated.

question: If a game begins with four players and drops down to two remaining players over the course of play, does it stop being a "multiplayer game" for rules purposes once only two players are left?
answer_gold: No. Whether a game counts as multiplayer is fixed by how many players it began with, not by how many are currently still in it. A game that began with four players stays a multiplayer game even after it's down to its last two combatants -- for example, its starting player would still not skip their first-turn draw step under the two-player rule, since that rule only applies to games that began with exactly two players.

cr_quotes.800.1: A multiplayer game is a game that begins with more than two players.

question: If two different players each control a separate instance of the same triggered ability, and both instances trigger off the same shared event, is it guaranteed that one specific player's version resolves before the other's, or could either one happen first depending on choices made?
answer_gold: It's guaranteed, not a free choice between the two players. APNAP order fixes it: the active player's copy of the trigger is placed on the stack first (ending up underneath), and each nonactive player's copy goes on afterward (ending up on top). Since the stack resolves top-down, a nonactive player's version of a shared trigger always resolves before the active player's version does, regardless of what either player would prefer.

cr_quotes.603.3b: First, each player, in APNAP order, puts each triggered ability they control with a trigger condition that isn't another ability triggering on the stack in any order they choose.
cr_quotes.405.5: 405.5. When all players pass in succession, the top (last-added) spell or ability on the stack resolves. If the stack is empty when all players pass, the current step or phase ends and the next begins.

question: When a spell is cast in response to another spell already on the stack, which one actually resolves first?
answer_gold: The newer one -- the spell cast "in response to" an earlier spell or ability goes on top of the stack and resolves first, before the original spell or ability it responded to gets a chance to resolve. The stack always resolves its top (most recently added) object first once all players pass in succession.

cr_quotes.117.7: If a player with priority casts a spell or activates an activated ability while another spell or ability is already on the stack, the new spell or ability has been cast or activated "in response to" the earlier spell or ability. The new spell or ability will resolve first.
cr_quotes.405.5: When all players pass in succession, the top (last-added) spell or ability on the stack resolves.

question: If an object checks whether a spell or ability "targets only" a single object or player, does it matter how many separate instances of the word "target" that spell used to point at the same object, or does it only care that a single distinct object/player was chosen overall?
answer_gold: It only cares about the number of distinct objects or players chosen as targets, not how many times the word "target" was used to point at them. If a spell targets the same single object or player multiple times (once for each instance of the word "target" in its text), it still counts as "targeting only" that one object or player.

cr_quotes.115.9c: An object that looks for a "[spell or ability] that targets only [something]" checks the number of different objects or players that were chosen as targets of that spell or ability when it was put on the stack (as modified by effects that changed those targets), not the number of those objects or players that are currently legal targets. If that number is one (even if the spell or ability targets that object or player multiple times), the current state of that spell or ability's target is checked as described in rule 115.9b.

question: If a permanent's activated ability has a restriction like "activate only once each turn," and that permanent is then copied by a fresh copy effect after the ability has already been used up for the turn, does the new copy inherit the used-up restriction, or does it start the turn fresh?
answer_gold: The new copy starts fresh and can use the ability again this turn. A "once each turn" restriction is tracked per object, and it does keep following an object even if that object's controller changes -- but a copy created by a copy effect is a brand-new object with no memory of its previous existence, so it isn't the same object that already used the ability and hasn't used its own copy of that restricted ability yet this turn.

cr_quotes.602.5b: If an activated ability has a restriction on its use (for example, "Activate only once each turn"), the restriction continues to apply to that object even if its controller changes.
cr_quotes.707.2: The copiable values are the values derived from the text printed on the object...
cr_quotes.400.7: An object that moves from one zone to another becomes a new object with no memory of, or relation to, its previous existence.
cr_quotes.403.4: 403.4. Whenever a permanent enters the battlefield, it becomes a new object and has no relationship to any previous permanent represented by the same card, except for the cases listed in rule 400.7. (This is also true for any objects entering any zone.)

question_flag: The restriction-tracking rule (602.5b) only explicitly addresses a control change, not a fresh copy being created via a copy effect while the original permanent stays on the battlefield unaffected. I'm inferring that a copy is a distinct object (per 400.7 and the general copy-effect framework in 707) and therefore has its own independent usage count, which matches the rulesguru answer for rg1063's Mirage Mirror scenario, but I did not find a rule stating this for copies specifically (as opposed to zone changes or control changes).
